analysis.one_liner: Lets states, not the EPA, run the permit programs for coal ash dumps.
analysis.headline: The bill, backed by 12 cosponsors from both parties, never got a committee markup or Senate vote and died when the 112th Congress ended in January 2013.
analysis.plain_summary: Coal-burning power plants produce millions of tons of coal ash, which is stored in ponds and landfills that can leak into groundwater. This bill would have written the rules for handling that ash into law as a state-run permit system: each state could adopt its own program meeting federal minimum standards, and the EPA would step in only if a state refused or failed to fix deficiencies. It would also have locked in the EPA's 2000 decision that coal ash is not hazardous waste, keeping it out of the stricter hazardous-waste rules.
analysis.who_benefits: Coal-burning electric utilities, which avoid a federal hazardous-waste designation for coal ash and the stricter design, liner, and cleanup requirements that would come with one. States gain control over permitting, and companies that recycle ash into concrete and wallboard keep it eligible for those uses.

how_it_helps.text: Replaces the prospect of federal EPA hazardous-waste rules for coal ash with state permit programs that meet federal minimum specifications, with the EPA stepping in only if a state opts out or fails to remedy deficiencies [S2].

Sets minimum requirements: structures must contain maximum waste volumes, new units must sit at least two feet above the water table, and groundwater monitoring, location restrictions, and financial assurance criteria apply [S2].
Prohibits any reading of the bill that would alter the EPA's 2000 determination that fossil fuel combustion wastes do not warrant hazardous-waste regulation [S3].
Excludes coal ash used or stored at surface mining and reclamation sites from any federal permit program, and lets states decline requirements they judge unnecessary [S2].

analysis.who_pays: People who live near coal ash ponds and landfills and drink from wells or use surface water nearby. States may waive criteria they decide are unnecessary, the EPA defers to states and intervenes only after a failure, and the bill locks out the stricter hazardous-waste route entirely.

drawbacks.text: A state may determine that specific criteria are 'not needed' and decline to apply them; the EPA can treat that as a deficiency only after the fact, meaning protections can be rolled back before any federal check [S2].
The EPA must defer to states and can implement its own program only in narrow cases: if a governor declines, a state fails to remedy deficiencies after notice, or a state quits its program [S3].
Existing dumps are held to weaker location standards than new ones, and the bill cannot be construed to bring coal ash under hazardous-waste regulation at all [S3].

A good-faith defense exists: the bill does impose a real permitting floor — containment, groundwater monitoring for specific pollutants, closure plans requiring liquid removal from impoundments — while preserving states' right to go stricter and citizens' right to sue [S3]. Supporters argued a federal hazardous-waste designation would kill the recycling of ash into concrete and wallboard.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill is not a free pass — it creates a national permitting floor where none existed in statute. But its core effect is to foreclose the stricter option: coal ash stays a non-hazardous waste, states can waive requirements they find inconvenient, and federal oversight kicks in only after a state program fails. For the communities living around hundreds of aging ash impoundments, that trade runs mainly in the industry's favor.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the Senate Environment and Public Works Committee the day it was introduced, never got a markup or a floor vote, and died when the Congress ended in January 2013.

narrative.text: Sen. John Hoeven introduced the bill on October 20, 2011 with a bipartisan group of cosponsors including senators from major coal states [S1].
It was read twice and referred to the Committee on Environment and Public Works that same day — the last action ever taken on it [S5].
No further action appears in the record; the committee never reported the bill and the Senate never voted on it before the 112th Congress ended on January 3, 2013 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because it died, coal-burning utilities did not get their state-run permit regime written into law — but the public also got nothing from Congress on coal ash this session. The practical winner was the status quo, with the EPA free to pursue its own coal ash rules and no statutory floor or statutory ceiling enacted.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: The status quo; utilities gained nothing yet

for.name: John Hoeven
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and recruited a bipartisan group of cosponsors from coal-producing states.

for.name: 12 Senate cosponsors
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, including senators from North Dakota, West Virginia, Louisiana, Nebraska, Ohio, Wyoming, and South Dakota.

against.name: Barbara Boxer
against.role: Chair, Senate Environment and Public Works Committee
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a committee markup or brought the bill to a vote, leaving it in committee until the Congress ended.

against.name: Environmental Protection Agency
against.role: Federal regulator of coal ash disposal
against.what_they_did: Was developing its own nationwide rules for coal ash disposal, which this bill would have displaced with state-run programs.

sides.party_line_note: Sponsorship was bipartisan — a Republican lead sponsor plus 5 Democratic and 7 Republican cosponsors, several from coal states — but the bill never reached a vote, so no roll call shows where the parties stood.

industries.note: The bill replaces the prospect of federal hazardous-waste rules with state permit programs, sparing utilities stricter federal liner, monitoring, and cleanup requirements for ash ponds and landfills. The cost of weaker oversight falls on communities near those sites whose groundwater is at risk.

The bill codifies the EPA's 2000 determination that coal combustion waste need not be regulated as hazardous and exempts ash placed at mine reclamation sites from federal permitting, keeping coal ash disposal cheap and supporting continued coal combustion.

industries.industry: Coal ash recyclers (concrete and wallboard makers)
industries.note: Keeping coal ash out of hazardous-waste regulation preserves its 'beneficial use' in products like concrete and wallboard, which supporters argued is genuinely useful — recycling ash displaces mined raw materials. The gain depends on keeping the non-hazardous designation.

States become the permanent permitting channel for coal ash, with the federal government stepping in only when a state opts out or fails. States also keep the right to adopt stricter rules than the federal floor.
